Backbiter
BAK-by-ter
noun
From back and bite — one who bites at the back, who tears at a man where he cannot see nor defend himself, as a cur snaps at the heel of a passer-by. It renders the Greek katalalos, “a speaker-against,” and the Hebrew ragal, “to go about on foot” as a spy or slanderer.

Biblical Definition

A backbiter is one who speaks evil of a man behind his back — who tears at his name where he cannot answer, as a dog bites the heel of one already gone by; the wound is in the back, and the bite is real. Where the whisperer works secretly in the ear, the backbiter speaks out; the Greek katalalos is simply a speaker-against, an open evil-speaker who wants no cover but the absence of his victim. David sets the sin at the door of God’s house: asking who shall abide in the LORD’s tabernacle, he answers, “He that backbiteth not with his tongue, nor doeth evil to his neighbour, nor taketh up a reproach against his neighbour” (Psa 15:3) — and taking up a reproach is condemned with the making of it. He who repeats an evil report is a backbiter though the tale be none of his coining. Solomon prescribes the remedy: “The north wind driveth away rain: so doth an angry countenance a backbiting tongue” (Pro 25:23). A cold look scatters the evil-speaker as the north wind scatters the clouds; he speaks because he is welcomed, and a face that refuses to be entertained will shut his mouth faster than an argument. Paul places backbiters in the roll of the reprobate mind, hard by the haters of God (Rom 1:30). And David, setting the rule of his own house, will not have such a man about him at all: “Whoso privily slandereth his neighbour, him will I cut off: him that hath an high look and a proud heart will not I suffer” (Psa 101:5). The bite is no less a wound because the wounded man never sees the teeth.

Webster 1828 Definition

One who speaks evil of an absent man; a secret calumniator, who tears at a name behind its owner’s back.

expand to see more

BACKBITER, a secret calumniator; one who censures or reproaches an absent person.

From back and bite: the wound is given where a man cannot see nor defend himself.

It renders the Greek katalalos, a speaker-against — the open evil-speaker, as distinct from the whisperer.

He that backbiteth not is marked among the dwellers in God’s tabernacle (Psa 15:3).

An angry countenance drives away a backbiting tongue as the north wind drives away rain (Pro 25:23).

Key Scripture

Psa 15:3 — "He that backbiteth not with his tongue, nor doeth evil to his neighbour, nor taketh up a reproach against his neighbour."

Pro 25:23 — "The north wind driveth away rain: so doth an angry countenance a backbiting tongue."

Rom 1:30 — "Backbiters, haters of God, despiteful, proud, boasters, inventors of evil things, disobedient to parents,"

Psa 101:5 — "Whoso privily slandereth his neighbour, him will I cut off: him that hath an high look and a proud heart will not I suffer."

Modern Corruption

Live: the age keeps the bite and drops the name, calling it candour, venting, or telling it like it is — and it counts the hearer innocent.

expand to see more

Backbiting has kept every one of its teeth and lost only its ugly name. It is now candour, or venting, or refusing to pretend, or simply telling it like it is; and a generation that would be scandalized to be called a slanderer will spend an hour tearing at a brother’s reputation and call it honesty. But honesty is not the question. A thing may be true and still be a bite, if it is spoken where the man cannot answer and to hearers who cannot help. That is why Psa 15:3 does not ask whether the report is accurate: it asks whether thou hast taken up a reproach against thy neighbour. Paul’s catalogue is more sobering still. Backbiters stand in Rom 1:30 next to haters of God and inventors of evil things — not because a sharp word equals blasphemy in its measure, but because the tongue that will not spare a brother has learned its appetite in the same fallen heart.

The principle to recover is that the ear is as guilty as the mouth, and the cure is in the face. David condemns him that taketh up a reproach as well as him that makes it; the man who forwards the evil report has bitten his neighbour with borrowed teeth. And Solomon does not tell us to argue the backbiter down — he tells us to look at him: “The north wind driveth away rain: so doth an angry countenance a backbiting tongue.” The evil-speaker speaks because he is entertained. A grave face, an unamused silence, a plain word that this man is not here to answer for himself, and the clouds scatter. The saints who mean to have peace in the church will not answer backbiting with backbiting; they will simply decline to be its weather.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

The word means one who bites at the back — who speaks evil of an absent man.

expand to see more

Backbiter — from back and bite, one who bites where a man cannot see.

The picture is a cur snapping at the heel of one already passed by.

It renders the Greek katalalos, “a speaker-against,” the open evil-speaker.

He is barred from the tabernacle of the LORD (Psa 15:3).

An angry countenance drives him away as the north wind drives rain (Pro 25:23).

Usage

"He that backbiteth not with his tongue shall abide in the tabernacle of the LORD."

"To take up a reproach is to bite with borrowed teeth — the hearer is no innocent."

"As the north wind driveth away rain, so an angry countenance shuts a backbiting tongue."
